Subject: Scheduling challenge for a multi‑mode, resource‑constrained project

Overview
We are preparing the baseline schedule for a project composed of multiple interdependent activities that must share limited, renewable resources and a fixed spending cap. Each activity can be executed in one of several modes that trade time for cost. Our aim is to complete the project as early as possible while honoring all timing relationships, resource-sharing limits, and the overall budget.

Execution modes and tradeoffs
- Every activity must be planned in exactly one execution mode.
- Each mode has a distinct duration, resource usage profile, and cost. Faster modes shorten the timeline but are more expensive and may use more resources.
- Once an activity starts, it runs to completion without interruption; mode choices and start times must be set accordingly.

Dependencies and timing controls
- Activities follow precedence relationships: specified predecessors must finish before successors can start.
- Some dependencies require a minimum wait between finishing a predecessor and starting its successor (minimum delays).
- Certain dependencies also require that the successor start within a maximum window after the predecessor finishes (maximum delays).
- Some activities have earliest allowable start times (release dates), and some have hard deadlines by which they must be completed.

Renewable resources and the conservative safety rule
- The project uses multiple renewable resource types with fixed capacities. When an activity finishes, the resources it used become available for other work.
- To manage potential overload caused by mode choices, we use a conservative safety rule for unrelated activities (i.e., activities not connected by precedence):
  • If there exists at least one combination of their modes and at least one resource for which their combined usage would exceed that resource’s capacity, the two activities must not overlap in time. They must be sequenced—one finishes before the other starts.
  • This rule is deliberately cautious: even if some mode pairs would fit, the mere possibility of exceeding capacity in any mode pairing means the scheduler must set an order.
  • This is our only capacity safeguard. We do not perform a separate, continuous “at-all-times” capacity check beyond these pairwise sequencing decisions.

Budget cap
- The project has a fixed overall budget. The sum of costs for the selected modes across all activities must not exceed this cap.
- This creates a tradeoff: accelerating critical work with faster (and costlier) modes can shorten the schedule, but total spending must remain within the budget.

Planning implications
- We must choose the mode for each activity and sequence the work so that:
  • All precedence links and minimum/maximum delay requirements are respected.
  • Activities start no earlier than their release dates and finish before any hard deadlines.
  • The conservative sequencing rule prevents overlapping of any independent activity pair that could, in any mode combination, exceed a resource capacity.
  • The total cost of the chosen modes does not exceed the budget.
- These choices interact. For example, speeding up one path may force additional sequencing elsewhere due to the safety rule, and budget limits may prevent using accelerated modes across the board.

Goal
Schedule all activities—selecting a single mode for each and sequencing start times—to minimize the total project duration (makespan) while staying within the budget and adhering to all timing and resource-sharing constraints.

Next steps
- Confirm the activity set, resource capacities, available modes, and all timing constraints listed in the annex.
- Generate and review candidate schedules that balance cost and time, highlighting where the safety rule forces sequencing of otherwise independent work.
- Align on a preferred plan that meets the budget and achieves the shortest feasible completion date.
